controls.discussion: This control addresses the establishment of policy and procedures for the effective implementation of selected security controls and control enhancements in the AC family. Policy and procedures reflect applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines. Security program policies and procedures at the organization level may make the need for system-specific policies and procedures unnecessary. The policy can be included as part of the general information security policy for organizations or conversely, can be represented by multiple policies reflecting the complex nature of certain organizations. The procedures can be established for the security program in general and for particular systems, if needed. The organizational risk management strategy is a key factor in establishing policy and procedures.

controls.discussion: The identification of authorized users of the system and the specification of access privileges reflects the requirements in other controls in the security plan. Users requiring administrative privileges on information systems and components are identified. Accounts may be individual, shared, or group accounts. Shared and group accounts are considered when organizations need to support multiple users with the same privilege level. Identifying authorized users involves the determination of which individuals are eligible for particular account types. Account management includes the identification and selection of appropriate account types for organizational users. Organizations use different types of accounts including individual, shared, group, system, service, anonymous, emergency, developer, temporary, and guest/anonymous accounts. Shared accounts may represent a security risk in some situations since the activities of any user with access to such an account may not be individually attributable. Organizations consider the risk associated with using shared accounts and establish procedures to mitigate that risk when it is deemed necessary.

controls.title: Access Enforcement
controls.statement: Enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information and system resources in accordance with applicable access control policies.
controls.discussion: Access control policies—such as identity-based policies, role-based policies, and attribute-based policies—and access enforcement mechanisms—such as access control lists, access control matrices, and cryptography—are employed by organizations to control access between users (or processes acting on behalf of users) and objects (e.g., devices, files, records, processes, programs, domains) in systems. In addition to enforcing authorized access at the system level and recognizing that systems can host many applications and services in support of organizational missions and business operations, access enforcement mechanisms can also be employed at the application and service level to provide increased information security and privacy.

controls.title: Information Flow Enforcement
controls.statement: Enforce approved authorizations for controlling the flow of information within the system and between connected systems based on [Assignment: organization-defined information flow control policies].
controls.discussion: Information flow control regulates where information can travel within a system and between systems (as opposed to who can access the information) and without explicit regard to subsequent accesses to that information. Flow control restrictions include keeping export-controlled information from being transmitted in the clear to the internet, blocking outside traffic that claims to be from within the organization, restricting requests to the internet that are not from the internal web proxy server, and limiting information transfers between organizations based on data structures and content. Transferring information between systems representing different security domains with different security policies introduces the risk that such transfers violate one or more domain security policies. In such situations, information owners/stewards provide guidance at designated policy enforcement points between connected systems.

controls.title: Separation of Duties

items.label: AC-5a: Identify and document [Assignment: organization-defined duties of individuals requiring separation]; and
items.text: Identify and document [Assignment: organization-defined duties of individuals requiring separation]; and

items.label: AC-5b: Define system access authorizations to support separation of duties.
items.text: Define system access authorizations to support separation of duties.

controls.discussion: The separation of duties addresses the potential for abuse of authorized privileges and helps to reduce the risk of malevolent activity without collusion. The separation of duties includes dividing mission functions and system support functions among different individuals or roles; conducting system support functions with different individuals; and ensuring that security personnel administering access control functions do not also administer audit functions. Because separation of duties can be difficult to implement in small organizations, compensating controls can be considered to reduce risk from insider threats.

controls.title: Least Privilege
controls.statement: Employ the principle of least privilege, allowing only authorized accesses for users (or processes acting on behalf of users) that are necessary to accomplish assigned organizational tasks.
controls.discussion: The principle of least privilege is applied with the goal of authorized privileges no greater than necessary to accomplish required organizational missions or business functions. Organizations consider the creation of additional processes, roles, and system accounts as necessary to achieve least privilege. Organizations also apply least privilege to the development, implementation, and operation of organizational systems. Security functions include establishing system accounts, configuring access authorizations (i.e., permissions, privileges), setting events to be audited, and setting intrusion detection parameters. Security-relevant information includes filtering rules for routers and firewalls, configuration parameters for security services, cryptographic key management information, and access control lists.

items.label: AC-7a: Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
items.text: Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and

controls.discussion: This control applies regardless of whether the login occurs via a local or network connection. Due to the potential for denial-of-service attacks, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined time period established by organizations. If a delay algorithm is selected, organizations may employ different algorithms for different components of the system based on the capabilities of those components. Responses to unsuccessful login attempts may be implemented at the operating system and application levels. Organizations can address the concerns about protecting credentials from brute force attacks by implementing and enforcing organizational policy as part of the access control process.

controls.discussion: System use notifications can be implemented using messages or warning banners displayed before individuals log in to systems. System use notifications are used only for access via logon interfaces with human users and are not required when such human interfaces do not exist. Based on an assessment of risk, organizations consider whether or not a secondary sign-in warning is needed to access applications or other system resources after the initial network logon. Organizations consider system use notification messages and warning banners displayed in multiple languages based on organizational needs and the demographics of system users. Organizations also consult with the Office of the General Counsel for legal review and approval of warning banner content.

controls.title: Previous Logon Notification
controls.statement: Notify the user, upon successful logon to the system, of the date and time of the last logon.
controls.discussion: This control is applicable to system logons via human interfaces to the system. Organizations can use the information from AC-9 to help detect unauthorized system use. Notification is applicable to both successful and unsuccessful logon attempts and provides additional information to users about the security attributes of the system. Organizations determine the granularity and type of information provided as part of notifications based on an organizational assessment of risk.

controls.title: Concurrent Session Control
controls.statement: Limit the number of concurrent sessions for each system account to [Assignment: organization-defined number of sessions].
controls.discussion: Organizations may define the maximum number of concurrent sessions for system accounts globally, by account type, by account, or by a combination. For example, organizations may limit the number of concurrent sessions for system administrators or individuals processing particularly sensitive information to one session at a time. Concurrent session control addresses concurrent sessions for system accounts and does not address concurrent sessions by single users via multiple system accounts.

controls.title: Device Lock

items.label: AC-11a: Prevent further access to the system by [Selection (one or more): initiating a device lock after [Assignment: organization-defined time period] of inactivity; requiring the user to initiate a device lock before leaving the system unattended]; and
items.text: Prevent further access to the system by [Selection (one or more): initiating a device lock after [Assignment: organization-defined time period] of inactivity; requiring the user to initiate a device lock before leaving the system unattended]; and

items.label: AC-11b: Retain the device lock until the user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.
items.text: Retain the device lock until the user reestablishes access using established identification and authentication procedures.

controls.discussion: A device lock is a temporary action taken when a user stops working and moves away from the immediate physical vicinity of the information system but does not want to log out because of the temporary nature of the absence. An automatic device lock is initiated after a fixed time period of user inactivity. Device locks are implemented at the operating system level or can be implemented by other components of the system for virtual systems. Device locks are not a substitute for logging out of the system, for example, when organizations require users to log out at the end of workdays.

controls.title: Session Termination
controls.statement: Automatically terminate a user session after [Assignment: organization-defined conditions, or trigger events requiring session disconnect].
controls.discussion: Automatic session termination addresses the termination of user-initiated logical sessions in contrast to the termination of network connections that are associated with communications sessions. A logical session for a database application (for example) may not involve a network connection. End conditions for activating automatic session termination include organization-defined periods of user inactivity, targeted responses to certain types of incidents, and time-of-day restrictions on information access.

controls.discussion: Identification and authentication of users are not required for certain accesses to systems. Organizations identify which system accesses do not require identification or authentication consistent with applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, standards, and guidelines. Public websites or applications where individuals access information without identifying themselves would be an example where unauthenticated access is permitted.

controls.discussion: Security and privacy attributes are abstractions that represent the basic properties or characteristics of an entity with respect to safeguarding information or the privacy of individuals. These attributes are associated with specific information in storage, in process, and in transmission so that these attributes can be used as the basis for automated policy actions, human review, consent decisions, or other access decisions. The assignment of attributes to information and information systems is an organization-wide activity with the objective of identifying the types of attributes required for the organization to conduct its essential operations and business functions. The catalog of security and privacy attributes is reviewed and updated periodically to ensure that it remains sufficient and relevant. Attributes may be used to implement and support risk management policies such as access control policy, information flow control policy, and separation of duties policy.

controls.title: Remote Access

items.label: AC-17a: Establish and document usage restrictions, configuration/connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of remote access allowed; and
items.text: Establish and document usage restrictions, configuration/connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of remote access allowed; and

items.label: AC-17b: Authorize each type of remote access to the system prior to allowing such connections.
items.text: Authorize each type of remote access to the system prior to allowing such connections.

controls.discussion: Remote access is access to organizational systems by users (or processes acting on behalf of users) communicating through external networks. Types of remote access include dial-up, broadband, and wireless. Organizations use encrypted virtual private networks (VPNs) to enhance confidentiality and integrity over remote connections. Organizations use intrusion-detection and prevention systems as well as spam and malware protection in remote access systems. Remote access connections between cloud service providers and organizations are addressed as external system connections. The use of mobile code (i.e., code downloaded and executed on client devices from servers accessed via remote connections) requires appropriate security controls to prevent compromise of organizational systems.

controls.title: Wireless Access

items.label: AC-18a: Establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of wireless access; and
items.text: Establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for each type of wireless access; and

items.label: AC-18b: Authorize each type of wireless access to the system prior to allowing such connections.
items.text: Authorize each type of wireless access to the system prior to allowing such connections.

controls.discussion: Wireless technologies include microwave, packet radio (ultra-high frequency or very high frequency), 802.11x, and Bluetooth. Wireless networks use authentication protocols such as EAP/TLS and PEAP as well as encryption such as TKIP and CCMP, and organizations use firewalls, intrusion detection and prevention systems, and other mechanisms to protect wireless networks. Organizations consider the use of monitoring technologies such as wireless intrusion detection systems to provide situational awareness.

controls.title: Access Control for Mobile Devices
controls.objective_name: AC-19: Access Control for Mobile Devices

items.label: AC-19a: Establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for organization-controlled mobile devices, to include when such devices are outside of controlled areas; and
items.text: Establish configuration requirements, connection requirements, and implementation guidance for organization-controlled mobile devices, to include when such devices are outside of controlled areas; and

items.label: AC-19b: Authorize the connection of mobile devices to organizational systems.
items.text: Authorize the connection of mobile devices to organizational systems.

controls.discussion: A mobile device is a computing device that has a small form factor such that it can easily be carried by a single individual; is designed to operate without a physical connection; possesses local, non-removable or removable data storage; and includes a self-contained power source. Mobile device functionality may also include voice communication capabilities, on-board sensors that allow the devices to capture information, and/or built-in features for synchronizing local data with remote locations. Examples include smart phones and tablets. Mobile devices are typically associated with a single individual. The processing, storage, and transmission capability of the mobile device may be comparable to or merely a subset of notebook/desktop systems, depending on the nature and intended purpose of the device.

controls.discussion: This control addresses the use of external systems for processing, storage, or transmission of organizational information. For some categories of information, organizations prohibit the use of external systems entirely. In other situations, the use of external systems is permitted if the appropriate agreements are in place. The terms and conditions for the use of external systems are consistent with any trust relationships established with those systems and reflect the level of risk tolerance of the organization.

items.label: AC-21a: Enable authorized users to determine whether access authorizations assigned to a sharing partner match the information’s access and use restrictions for [Assignment: organization-defined information sharing circumstances where user discretion is required]; and
items.text: Enable authorized users to determine whether access authorizations assigned to a sharing partner match the information’s access and use restrictions for [Assignment: organization-defined information sharing circumstances where user discretion is required]; and

items.text: Employ [Assignment: organization-defined automated mechanisms or manual processes] to assist users in making information sharing and collaboration decisions.

controls.discussion: While organizations are required to adhere to applicable information sharing policy and cooperate with information sharing decisions, the sharing partner may have decision-making authority about information sharing in their own processes. Organizations employ a variety of mechanisms for making information sharing decisions including data use agreements, information sharing agreements, and information sharing requirements. The mechanisms employed by organizations to support information sharing decisions also reflect the importance of protecting the information and ensuring that appropriate controls are in place to protect such information.

items.label: AC-22a: Designate individuals authorized to make information publicly accessible

items.text: Review the content on the publicly accessible system for nonpublic information [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and remove such information, if discovered.

controls.discussion: In addition to the publicly accessible content of organizational websites, organizations also need to protect nonpublic information associated with the publicly accessible portions of their websites. Nonpublic information on publicly accessible websites includes, for example, scripts, comments within scripts, and certain metadata.

controls.title: Data Mining Protection
controls.statement: Employ [Assignment: organization-defined data mining prevention and detection techniques] for [Assignment: organization-defined data storage objects] to adequately detect and protect against data mining.
controls.discussion: Data mining is an analytical process that attempts to find correlations or patterns in large data sets for the purpose of data or knowledge discovery. Data storage objects include databases, database records, and database fields. Data mining prevention and detection techniques include limiting the types of responses provided to database queries, limiting the number/frequency of database queries to increase the work factor needed to determine the contents of databases, notifying organizational personnel when atypical database queries or accesses occur, and using neural networks or other pattern-based software tools to identify atypical access to organizational information.

controls.title: Access Control Decisions
controls.statement: a. Establish procedures to ensure [Assignment: organization-defined access control decisions] are applied to each access request prior to access enforcement; and b. Designate [Assignment: organization-defined individuals] to review and approve access control decisions.
controls.discussion: Access control decisions (also known as authorization decisions) occur when authorization information is applied to specific accesses. In contrast, access enforcement occurs when access control decisions are implemented. While it is very common to combine access control decision and enforcement in the same system component or mechanism, it is not required, and organizations can implement access control decisions and enforcement in different locations and by different components or mechanisms. For distributed systems, access control decisions may occur in separate components from those enforcing the access, and access control decisions and enforcement may be separated from mechanisms that generate access control information. In such instances, organizations require coordination to ensure that access control information is consistent and that access enforcement based on such information is accurate.

controls.title: Reference Monitor
controls.statement: Implement a reference monitor for [Assignment: organization-defined access control policies] that is tamperproof, always invoked, and small enough to be subject to analysis and testing, the completeness of which can be assured.
controls.discussion: A reference monitor is a set of design requirements on a reference validation mechanism (i.e., a mechanism that implements access control policy) that, as a key component of an operating system, mediates all accesses to objects by subjects. A reference monitor is tamperproof if it is protected from unauthorized modification or the circumvention of its access control policies. A reference monitor is always invoked if it mediates all accesses to objects regardless of the origin of the access request. A reference monitor is small enough to be subject to analysis and testing if it is sufficiently simple so that its implementation can be analyzed and tested to ensure that it is correct in its implementation of its access control policies.

controls.discussion: This control addresses the establishment of policy and procedures for the effective implementation of selected security controls and control enhancements in the AT family. Policy and procedures reflect applicable laws, executive orders, directives, regulations, policies, standards, and guidelines. Security program policies and procedures at the organization level may make the need for system-specific policies and procedures unnecessary. The policy can be included as part of the general information security policy for organizations or conversely, can be represented by multiple policies reflecting the complex nature of certain organizations. controls.discussion: An event is any observable occurrence in an organizational system. Organizations identify audit events as those events that are significant and relevant to the security of systems and the privacy of individuals and the environments in which those systems operate in order to meet specific and ongoing audit needs. Audit events can include password changes, failed logons or failed accesses related to systems, administrative privilege usage, use of PIV credentials, data action requests by data subjects, or third-party credential usage. In determining event types, organizations consider the auditing appropriate for each of the security controls to be implemented. To balance auditing requirements with other system needs, this control also requires identifying that subset of event types that are audited at any given point in time.

controls.discussion: Audit record content that may be necessary to satisfy this control includes time stamps, source and destination addresses, user or process identifiers, event descriptions, success or fail indications, filenames involved, and access control or flow control rules invoked. Event outcomes can include indicators of event success or failure and event-specific results such as the security state of the system after the event occurred. Detailed information that organizations may consider in audit records includes full-text recording of privileged commands or the individual identities of group account users. Organizations consider limiting the additional audit log information to only that information explicitly needed for specific audit requirements.

controls.discussion: Organizations consider the types of auditing to be performed and the audit processing requirements when allocating audit log storage capacity. Allocating sufficient audit log storage capacity reduces the likelihood of such capacity being exceeded and resulting in the potential loss or reduction of auditing capability.

controls.discussion: Audit logging process failures include software and hardware errors, failures in the audit log capturing mechanisms, and reaching or exceeding audit log storage capacity. Organization-defined actions to be taken in response to audit logging process failures can include graceful degradation, halting the system, mirroring and maintaining audit logs on backup systems, alerting organizational personnel, and using alternative audit logging mechanisms.

Findings can be reported to organizational entities including the incident response team, help desk, and information security officers.

Audit reduction and report generation capabilities do not always emanate from the same system or from the same organizational entities conducting auditing activities.

controls.discussion: Time stamps generated by organizational systems include date and time. Time is expressed in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), a modern continuation of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT), or local time with an offset from UTC. Granularity of time measurements refers to the degree of synchronization between system clocks and reference clocks such as clocks synchronizing within hundreds of milliseconds or within tens of milliseconds.

controls.discussion: Unauthorized read access to audit information could indicate that an adversary has obtained access to audit data and could indicate a potential compromise of audit activities. Unauthorized creation, modification, or deletion of audit information could obstruct, disable, mislead, or otherwise undermine the integrity of the audit trail. Audit information includes all information, such as audit records, audit settings, audit reports, and personally identifiable information needed to successfully audit system activity. Audit logging tools are those programs and devices used to conduct system audit and logging activities.

controls.discussion: Non-repudiation protects against false claims by users who deny having performed a particular action. Non-repudiation services can be used to determine if information originated from an individual or if an individual took specific actions (e.g., sending an email, signing a contract, approving a procurement request, or receiving specific information). Organizations obtain non-repudiation services by employing various tools, techniques, and mechanisms including digital signatures and digital message receipts.

controls.discussion: Organizations retain audit records until it is determined that such records are no longer needed for administrative, legal, audit, or other operational purposes. This includes, for example, retention and availability of audit records relative to freedom of information act requests, subpoenas, and law enforcement actions. Organizations develop standard categories of audit records relative to such legal and operational requirements and standard response processes for each type of record. The National Archives and Records Administration provides guidance on records retention.

controls.discussion: A continuous monitoring strategy and an ongoing continuous monitoring program can facilitate cost-effective, risk-based decisions regarding the security and privacy posture of organizational systems. Continuous monitoring programs facilitate ongoing awareness of threats, vulnerabilities, and information security and privacy to support organizational risk management decisions. The terms continuous and ongoing imply that organizations assess and analyze security and privacy controls and information security and privacy risks at a frequency sufficient to support risk-based decisions. The results of continuous monitoring programs generate appropriate risk response actions by organizations. Organizations establish tolerance thresholds for acceptable risk and analyze security assessment information collected through continuous monitoring activities to determine when risk levels exceed organizational tolerances.

controls.discussion: Penetration testing is a specialized form of assessment conducted on systems or individual system components to identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited by adversaries. Such testing can be used to either validate the effectiveness of security controls or to identify residual vulnerabilities. Organizations can use penetration testing during the assessment process to check for vulnerabilities in systems. Penetration testing methodologies differ in the amount of information provided to testers about the systems being assessed.

Organizations consider the risks that may be introduced when systems are connected to other systems with different security requirements and security controls, both within organizations and external to organizations. Authorizing officials determine the risk associated with system interconnections and the appropriate controls employed. Organizations typically do not have complete control over external systems and the controls employed therein.

Baseline configurations serve as a basis for future builds, releases, and/or changes to systems and include information about system components, network topology, and the logical placement of components in the system architecture. Maintaining baseline configurations requires creating new baselines as organizational systems change over time. Organizations consider the impact of security during configuration management activities and ensure that systems maintain required security postures over time.

controls.discussion: Configuration change control for organizational systems involves the systematic proposal, justification, implementation, testing, review, and disposition of changes to the systems, including system upgrades and modifications. Configuration change control includes changes to baseline configurations for components and configuration items of systems, changes to configuration settings for information technology products (e.g., operating systems, applications, firewalls, routers, and cryptographic modules), and changes to remediate unplanned outages.

controls.title: Impact Analyses
controls.statement: Analyze changes to the system to determine potential security and privacy impacts prior to change implementation.
controls.discussion: Organizational personnel with information security and privacy responsibilities (e.g., system administrators, system security officers, system security engineers, and privacy officers) conduct security and privacy impact analyses. Individuals conducting security and privacy impact analyses possess the necessary skills and technical expertise to analyze the changes to systems and the associated security and privacy ramifications. Security and privacy impact analysis may include reviewing security and privacy plans to understand security and privacy requirements and reviewing system design documentation to understand the implementation of security and privacy controls.

controls.title: Access Restrictions for Change
controls.statement: Define, document, approve, and enforce physical and logical access restrictions associated with changes to the system.
controls.discussion: Any changes to the hardware, software, or firmware components of systems can potentially have significant effects on the overall security of those systems. Therefore, organizations permit only qualified and authorized individuals to access systems for purposes of initiating changes, including upgrades and modifications. Access restrictions for change also include software libraries. Access restrictions include physical and logical access controls, workflow automation, media libraries, abstract layers (i.e., changes implemented into third-party interfaces rather than directly into systems), and change windows (i.e., changes occur only during specified times).

Organizations establish organization-wide configuration settings and subsequently derive specific configuration settings for systems. The established settings become part of the systems configuration baseline. Common secure configurations or hardening guides are available from a variety of public and private sector resources.

controls.discussion: Systems provide a wide variety of functions and services. Some of the functions and services routinely provided by default, may not be necessary to support essential organizational missions, functions, or operations. Additionally, it is sometimes the case that intended functionality provides security risks to the organization. In these situations, the cost of eliminating the functionality outweighs the risk of keeping it. Organizations can either disable the unnecessary capabilities or explicitly prohibit the use of such capabilities by issuing a policy statement to that effect.

Organizations may choose to implement centralized system component inventories that include components from multiple organizational systems. In such situations, organizations ensure that the inventories include system-specific information required for proper component accountability (e.g., system association, system owner). Information deemed necessary for effective accountability of system components includes hardware inventory specifications, software license information, software version numbers, component owners, and for networked components or devices, machine names and network addresses.

controls.discussion: Contingency planning for systems is part of an overall program for achieving continuity of operations for organizational operations and assets. Contingency plans address both information system restoration and implementation of alternative mission or business processes when systems are compromised. The effectiveness of contingency planning is maximized by considering such planning throughout the phases of the system development life cycle. Performing contingency planning on hardware, software, and firmware development can be an effective means of achieving system resiliency. Contingency plans reflect the degree to which organizations want to sustain system capabilities in emergencies.

Organizations have flexibility and discretion in the breadth, depth, and timelines of corrective actions.

Items covered by alternate storage site agreements include all types of information storage regardless of the physical form of the storage (e.g., paper records and digital data).

Items covered by alternate processing site agreements include system software and applications, system hardware, physical facilities, data and information, and trained personnel. Alternate processing sites reflect the requirements for continuity of operations and the possibility that primary sites may not be recoverable in the time period consistent with mission/business needs.

Organizations can employ information system mechanisms or organizational processes to conduct backups of critical information.

controls.discussion: Recovery is executing contingency plan activities to restore organizational missions or business functions. Reconstitution takes place following recovery and includes activities for returning systems to fully operational states. Recovery and reconstitution operations reflect mission and business priorities, recovery point/time and reconstitution objectives, and organizational metrics consistent with contingency plan requirements.

controls.title: Alternate Communications Protocols
controls.statement: Provide [Assignment: organization-defined alternative communications protocols] in support of maintaining continuity of operations.
controls.discussion: Contingency plans can include organizational priorities for the use of alternative communications protocols. Such protocols may be considered when addressing system failures to ensure the resumption of operations is prioritized.

controls.title: Safe Mode
controls.statement: When [Assignment: organization-defined conditions] are detected, enter a safe mode of operation with [Assignment: organization-defined restrictions on system operations].
controls.discussion: Safe mode allows systems to be placed in a configuration that minimizes capabilities. Safe mode may be invoked in response to unusual or atypical situations that could result in damage to the organization. This control is especially valuable for systems that support safety-critical operations or applications.

controls.title: Alternative Security Mechanisms
controls.statement: Employ [Assignment: organization-defined alternative or supplemental security mechanisms] for satisfying [Assignment: organization-defined security functions] when the primary means of implementing the security function is unavailable or compromised.
controls.discussion: Use of alternative security mechanisms supports system resiliency, sustained operations, and contingency planning. Organizations can employ compensating controls as alternative security mechanisms when the primary security mechanisms are unavailable or compromised.

controls.title: Identification and Authentication (Organizational Users)
controls.statement: Uniquely identify and authenticate organizational users and associate that unique identification with processes acting on behalf of those users.
controls.discussion: The requirement for this control is intended to apply to both the logon of the user to the system and the manner in which the user accesses system resources once logged on. Different types of users exist in an organizational system including employees, contractors, partners, and visitors. User accounts are identifiers for users that are created in the system. Users may have individual identifiers or shared (group) identifiers. Organizations use individual identifiers rather than group identifiers when feasible, to improve accountability and support auditing. Multifactor authentication (MFA) requires the use of at least two of the following authentication factors: something you know (e.g., password), something you have (e.g., a PKI certificate), or something you are (e.g., biometric).

controls.title: Device Identification and Authentication
controls.statement: Uniquely identify and authenticate [Assignment: organization-defined devices and/or types of devices] before establishing [Assignment: organization-defined type of connection or establishment of connection].
controls.discussion: Organizational systems typically boot from fixed media such as hard drives; fixed media generally contains an operating system image and target device configuration information. Device identification and authentication are required prior to data exchange with the target device. Authentication mechanisms vary with the characteristics of the device being authenticated. Devices that require identification and authentication include routers, switches, networked printers, VoIP phones, scanners, medical devices, and laboratory equipment.

Authenticator management is addressed in IA-5.

controls.discussion: Authenticators include passwords, cryptographic devices, biometrics, certificates, one-time password devices, and ID badges. Device authenticators include certificates and passwords. Initial authenticator content is the actual content of the authenticator (e.g., the initial password). In contrast, requirements for authenticator content are the characteristics or strength of the authenticator (e.g., minimum password length). Devices that need to be uniquely identified and authenticated are defined in IA-3. Authenticator management includes issuing and revoking (when no longer needed), authenticators for temporary access such as that required for remote maintenance. Additionally, for PKI-based authentication, organizations obtain authenticators from appropriate certification authorities.

controls.title: Authentication Feedback
controls.statement: Obscure feedback of authentication information during the authentication process to protect the information from possible exploitation and use by unauthorized individuals.
controls.discussion: The feedback from systems does not provide information that would allow unauthorized individuals to compromise authentication mechanisms. For some types of systems, such as kiosk systems or systems that do not involve human operators, feedback may not be an issue. The use of asterisks when masking passwords is an example of obscuring feedback.

controls.title: Cryptographic Module Authentication

controls.discussion: Authentication mechanisms may need to satisfy requirements in applicable laws, executive orders, directives, policies, standards, and guidelines. Cryptographic module authentication is handled in accordance with applicable federal laws, executive orders, directives, policies, standards, and guidelines.

controls.title: Identification and Authentication (Non-Organizational Users)
controls.statement: Uniquely identify and authenticate non-organizational users or processes acting on behalf of non-organizational users.
controls.discussion: Non-organizational users include system users other than organizational users explicitly covered by IA-2. These individuals are uniquely identified and authenticated for accesses other than those that are explicitly identified and documented in AC-14. In accordance with the E-Authentication E-Government initiative, authentication of non-organizational users accessing federal systems may be required to comply with NIST Special Publication 800-63, Electronic Authentication Guideline.

controls.title: Service Identification and Authentication
controls.statement: Uniquely identify and authenticate [Assignment: organization-defined system services and applications] before establishing communications with devices, users, or other services or applications.
controls.discussion: This control supports service-to-service communications and helps ensure that services are communicating with authorized parties. Service identification and authentication addresses communications between services, whether microservices in a service mesh, application programming interfaces (APIs), or any other type of service component. Organizations may also consider the use of strong authenticators (e.g., certificate-based) for services to support non-repudiation of service communications.

controls.title: Adaptive Authentication
controls.statement: Require individuals accessing the system to employ [Assignment: organization-defined supplemental authentication techniques or mechanisms] under specific [Assignment: organization-defined circumstances or situations].
controls.discussion: Adversaries may be able to defeat authentication mechanisms by employing specific attacks against those mechanisms. Organizations can use supplemental authentication techniques or mechanisms to address specific vulnerabilities through knowledge of how those attacks work. For example, organizations can use challenge questions to supplement password-based authentication mechanisms in cases where the password is suspected to have been compromised.

controls.title: Re-Authentication
controls.statement: Require users to re-authenticate when [Assignment: organization-defined circumstances or situations requiring re-authentication].
controls.discussion: Authentication requirements, including the need to re-authenticate individuals, are based on assessments of risk. Organizations may use risk-based approaches in assessing re-authentication requirements. Re-authentication of users is required to ensure that the security posture of the system is maintained.

controls.discussion: Identity proofing is the process of providing sufficient information (e.g., identity history, credentials, documents) that uniquely identifies a person as part of identity management. Organizations use identity proofing to establish, maintain, and manage identities for users in their systems. The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication 800-63A, Digital Identity Guidelines, provides guidance on identity proofing and enrollment.

For example, regular users may only need to know when and how to report problems, while system administrators may require additional training on how to handle or remediate incidents, and incident responders may need more extensive training on forensics, reporting mechanisms, communications, system recovery, and restoration.

controls.discussion: Organizations test incident response capabilities to determine the overall effectiveness of the capabilities and to identify potential weaknesses or deficiencies. Incident response testing includes the use of checklists, walk-through or tabletop exercises, simulations (both parallel and full interrupt), and comprehensive exercises. Incident response testing can also include a determination of the effects on organizational operations, assets, and individuals due to incident response.

Incident-related information can be obtained from a variety of sources including audit monitoring, network monitoring, physical access monitoring, user and administrator reports, and reported supply chain events.

controls.title: Incident Monitoring
controls.statement: Track and document incidents.
controls.discussion: Documenting incidents includes, for example, maintaining records about each incident, the status of the incident, and other pertinent information necessary for forensics, evaluating incident details, trends, and handling. Incident information can be obtained from a variety of sources including incident reports, incident response teams, audit monitoring, network monitoring, and physical access monitoring. Effective incident monitoring includes correlating incident information from multiple sources to achieve a comprehensive view of incidents in organizations.

Suspected security and privacy incidents include the receipt of suspicious email communications that can potentially contain malicious code. Incident information can inform risk assessments, control effectiveness assessments, security state assessments, and compliance. Organizations may report incidents to external entities including the United States Computer Emergency Readiness Team.

Information necessary for creating effective maintenance records includes the date and time of maintenance, a description of the maintenance performed, names of the individuals or group performing maintenance, name of escort (if applicable), and system components or equipment removed or replaced (including identification numbers, if applicable).

Authentication techniques used in the establishment of nonlocal maintenance and diagnostic sessions reflect the network access requirements in IA-2. Strong authentication requires authenticators that are resistant to replay attacks and employ multi-factor authentication. Strong authenticators include PKI where certificates are stored on a token protected by a password, passphrase, or biometric.

items.label: MA-5c: Designate organizational personnel with required access authorizations and technical competence to supervise the maintenance activities of personnel who do not possess the required access authorizations.
items.text: Designate organizational personnel with required access authorizations and technical competence to supervise the maintenance activities of personnel who do not possess the required access authorizations.

controls.discussion: Maintenance personnel refers to individuals who perform hardware or software maintenance on organizational systems, while the PE-2 control addresses physical access for individuals whose maintenance duties place them within the physical protection perimeter of the systems (i.e., within facilities). Technical competence of maintenance personnel refers to the maintenance qualifications of such personnel.

controls.title: Timely Maintenance
controls.statement: Obtain maintenance support and/or spare parts for [Assignment: organization-defined system components] within [Assignment: organization-defined time period] of failure.
controls.discussion: Preventive maintenance includes proactive care and servicing of systems for the purpose of maintaining equipment and facilities in satisfactory operating condition. Such maintenance provides for the systematic inspection, tests, measurements, adjustments, parts replacement, and cleaning of equipment and facilities. An important aspect of preventive maintenance is having the capability to obtain replacement parts when needed. Maintenance organizations address the risk of not having replacement parts by having adequate inventories of parts or components, or by negotiating contracts with vendors or suppliers ensuring expedited delivery of parts.

controls.title: Media Access
controls.statement: Restrict access to [Assignment: organization-defined types of digital and/or non-digital media] to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel or roles].
controls.discussion: System media includes both digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes diskettes, magnetic tapes, external and removable hard disk drives, flash/thumb drives, compact disks, and digital versatile disks. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm. Denying access to patient medical records in a community hospital to individuals other than the treating physician is an example implementing media access restrictions for non-digital media. Limiting access to the design specifications stored on compact disks in the media library to the project leader and the individuals on the development team are examples of restricting access to digital media.

controls.title: Media Marking

items.label: MP-3a: Mark system media indicating the distribution limitations, handling caveats, and applicable security markings (if any) of the information; and
items.text: Mark system media indicating the distribution limitations, handling caveats, and applicable security markings (if any) of the information; and

items.label: MP-3b: Exempt [Assignment: organization-defined types of system media] from marking if the media remain within [Assignment: organization-defined controlled areas].
items.text: Exempt [Assignment: organization-defined types of system media] from marking if the media remain within [Assignment: organization-defined controlled areas].

controls.discussion: The marking of sensitive system media addresses both protecting and controlling system media. The required markings are those consistent with applicable federal laws, executive orders, directives, policies, and regulations. Organizations apply markings to removable media and personnel use markings to ensure that the information in the media can be managed appropriately.

controls.title: Media Storage

items.label: MP-4a: Physically control and securely store [Assignment: organization-defined types of digital and/or non-digital media] within [Assignment: organization-defined controlled areas]; and
items.text: Physically control and securely store [Assignment: organization-defined types of digital and/or non-digital media] within [Assignment: organization-defined controlled areas]; and

items.label: MP-4b: Protect system media types defined in MP-4a until the media are destroyed or sanitized using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures.
items.text: Protect system media types defined in MP-4a until the media are destroyed or sanitized using approved equipment, techniques, and procedures.

controls.discussion: System media includes both digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes diskettes, magnetic tapes, external/removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, compact disks, and digital video disks. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm. An organizational assessment of risk guides the selection of media for storage, the type of protection employed, and the location of any such protected storage.

controls.title: Media Transport

items.label: MP-5a: Protect and control [Assignment: organization-defined types of system media] during transport outside of controlled areas using [Assignment: organization-defined controls]
items.text: Protect and control [Assignment: organization-defined types of system media] during transport outside of controlled areas using [Assignment: organization-defined controls]

items.text: Maintain accountability for system media during transport outside of controlled areas

items.text: Document activities associated with the transport of system media; and

items.label: MP-5d: Restrict the activities associated with the transport of system media to authorized personnel.
items.text: Restrict the activities associated with the transport of system media to authorized personnel.

controls.discussion: System media includes both digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes diskettes, magnetic tapes, external and removable hard drives, flash/thumb drives, compact disks, and digital video disks. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm. Protecting and controlling system media during transport includes restricting transport activities to authorized personnel, and encrypting information on digital media. Cryptographic mechanisms can provide confidentiality and integrity protections depending on the mechanisms implemented. Activities associated with transport include the actual transport as well as those activities such as releasing media for transport and ensuring that media enters the appropriate transport processes.

controls.title: Media Sanitization

items.label: MP-6a: Sanitize [Assignment: organization-defined system media] prior to disposal, release out of organizational control, or release for reuse using [Assignment: organization-defined sanitization techniques and procedures]; and
items.text: Sanitize [Assignment: organization-defined system media] prior to disposal, release out of organizational control, or release for reuse using [Assignment: organization-defined sanitization techniques and procedures]; and

items.label: MP-6b: Employ sanitization mechanisms with the strength and integrity commensurate with the security category or classification of the information.
items.text: Employ sanitization mechanisms with the strength and integrity commensurate with the security category or classification of the information.

controls.discussion: Media sanitization and disposal applies to all system media subject to disposal or reuse, whether or not the media is considered removable. Examples include media found in scanners, copiers, printers, notebook computers, workstations, network components, and mobile devices. The sanitization process removes information from the media such that the information cannot be retrieved or reconstructed. Sanitization techniques—including clearing, purging, cryptographic erase, and destruction—prevent the disclosure of information to unauthorized individuals when such media is reused or released for disposal.

controls.title: Media Use

items.label: MP-7a: [Selection: Restrict; Prohibit] the use of [Assignment: organization-defined types of system media] on [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components] using [Assignment: organization-defined controls]; and
items.text: [Selection: Restrict; Prohibit] the use of [Assignment: organization-defined types of system media] on [Assignment: organization-defined systems or system components] using [Assignment: organization-defined controls]; and

items.label: MP-7b: Prohibit the use of portable storage devices in organizational systems when such devices have no identifiable owner.
items.text: Prohibit the use of portable storage devices in organizational systems when such devices have no identifiable owner.

controls.discussion: System media includes both digital and non-digital media. Digital media includes diskettes, magnetic tapes, external and removable hard disk drives, flash/thumb drives, compact disks, and digital video disks. Non-digital media includes paper and microfilm. Removable media includes portable storage devices such as portable hard disk drives, digital video disks, compact disks, USB storage devices, and flash drives. Prohibiting the use of removable media in organizational systems provides an alternative to requiring organizations to sanitize such media before use on the systems.

controls.title: Media Downgrading

items.label: MP-8a: Establish [Assignment: organization-defined system media downgrading process] that includes employing downgrading mechanisms with strength and integrity commensurate with the security category or classification of the information
items.text: Establish [Assignment: organization-defined system media downgrading process] that includes employing downgrading mechanisms with strength and integrity commensurate with the security category or classification of the information

items.text: Identify [Assignment: organization-defined system media requiring downgrading]; and

items.label: MP-8d: Downgrade the identified system media using the established process.
items.text: Downgrade the identified system media using the established process.

controls.discussion: This control applies to digital media containing sensitive information. Organizations use trusted downgrade procedures to verify that downgraded media does not contain residual data above the classification level or high-water mark of the downgraded system. Downgrading of media is not always possible.

controls.discussion: Physical access restrictions apply to employees and visitors alike. Individuals with permanent physical access authorizations are not considered visitors. Organizations determine the types of facility access authorizations required which may include access by the type of physical space (e.g., office space, data centers, security rooms, access-controlled corridors), by specific systems within facilities, and by all systems within facilities. Physical access authorizations are distinct from logical access authorizations and are not used to manage information access.

items.label: PE-3a: Enforce physical access authorizations at [Assignment: organization-defined entry and exit points to the facility where the system resides] by: 1. Verifying individual access authorizations before granting access to the facility; and 2. Controlling ingress and egress to the facility using [Selection (one or more): [Assignment: organization-defined physical access control systems or devices]; guards]

items.text: Change combinations and keys [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and/or when keys are lost, combinations are compromised, or when individuals possessing the keys or combinations are transferred or terminated.

controls.discussion: Physical access controls apply to employees and visitors. Individuals with permanent physical access authorization credentials are not considered visitors. Access control systems can include identification cards, key cards, combination locks and card readers, and biometric readers. Organizations determine the strength of authorization credentials needed (including level of identity proofing) consistent with federal standards, policies, and procedures.

controls.title: Access Control for Transmission
controls.statement: Implement physical access controls to manage and protect [Assignment: organization-defined system distribution and transmission lines] within organizational facilities.
controls.discussion: Distribution and transmission lines refer to either internal or external networks and telecommunication lines. Organizations employ controls to protect transmission lines in their physical environments, for example, in raised floors beneath data centers. Selection of controls is commensurate with the risk of the environment.

controls.title: Access Control for Output Devices
controls.objective_name: PE-5: Access Control for Output Devices
controls.statement: Implement physical access controls to manage and protect [Assignment: organization-defined output devices] to prevent unauthorized individuals from obtaining the output.
controls.discussion: Controlling physical access to output devices includes placing output devices in locked rooms or other secured areas with keypad or card reader access controls, and allowing access to authorized individuals only. Placing printers, copiers, and fax machines in locations where access can be monitored reduces the risk of unauthorized individuals obtaining access to system output.

controls.title: Monitoring Physical Access

items.label: PE-6a: Monitor physical access to the facility where the system resides to detect and respond to physical security incidents
items.text: Monitor physical access to the facility where the system resides to detect and respond to physical security incidents

items.label: PE-6b: Review physical access logs [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and upon occurrence of [Assignment: organization-defined events or potential indications of events]; and
items.text: Review physical access logs [Assignment: organization-defined frequency] and upon occurrence of [Assignment: organization-defined events or potential indications of events]; and

items.label: PE-6c: Coordinate results of reviews and investigations with the organizational incident response capability.
items.text: Coordinate results of reviews and investigations with the organizational incident response capability.

controls.discussion: Organizational facilities include facilities that contain systems and the environments supporting those systems. Monitoring of physical access includes publicly accessible areas within organizational facilities such as visitor access areas and areas accessible to the public. This monitoring enables organizations to see individuals entering/exiting secured areas and potentially determine if authorized access is occurring.

controls.title: Visitor Access Records

items.label: PE-8a: Maintain visitor access records to the facility where the system resides for [Assignment: organization-defined time period]
items.text: Maintain visitor access records to the facility where the system resides for [Assignment: organization-defined time period]

items.label: PE-8b: Review visitor access records [Assignment: organization-defined frequency]; and
items.text: Review visitor access records [Assignment: organization-defined frequency]; and

items.label: PE-8c: Report anomalies in visitor access records to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel].
items.text: Report anomalies in visitor access records to [Assignment: organization-defined personnel].

controls.discussion: Organizations maintain visitor access records for a defined period. Visitor access records include the names and organizations of persons visiting, visitor signatures, forms of identification, dates of access, entry and departure times, purposes of visits, and names and signatures of responsible employees authorizing the visits.

controls.title: Power Equipment and Cabling
controls.statement: Protect power equipment and power cabling for the system from damage and destruction.
controls.discussion: Organizations determine the types of protection necessary for power equipment and cabling installed in different locations both internal and external to organizational facilities and environments of operation. This includes, for example, generators and uninterruptible power supplies. Power equipment and cabling in public areas, visitor areas, and areas accessible to the public may require additional protections.

controls.title: Emergency Shutoff

items.label: PE-10a: Provide the capability of shutting off power to [Assignment: organization-defined system or individual system components] in emergency situations
items.text: Provide the capability of shutting off power to [Assignment: organization-defined system or individual system components] in emergency situations

items.label: PE-10b: Place emergency shutoff switches or devices in [Assignment: organization-defined location by system or system component] to facilitate access for authorized personnel; and
items.text: Place emergency shutoff switches or devices in [Assignment: organization-defined location by system or system component] to facilitate access for authorized personnel; and

items.label: PE-10c: Protect emergency power shutoff capability from unauthorized activation.
items.text: Protect emergency power shutoff capability from unauthorized activation.

controls.discussion: Organizations can use manual, semi-automated, or automated emergency shutoff capabilities. Organizations maintain critical operational processes even when emergency shutoff switches are activated. Emergency lighting covers emergency exits and evacuation routes within facilities.

controls.title: Emergency Power
controls.statement: Provide an uninterruptible power supply to facilitate orderly, graceful degradation of system components in the event of a primary power source loss.
controls.discussion: An uninterruptible power supply (UPS) is an electrical apparatus that provides emergency power to a load when the input power source or mains power fails. An uninterruptible power supply differs from an auxiliary or standby power system or emergency power system in that it will provide near-instantaneous protection from input power interruptions by supplying energy stored in batteries, supercapacitors, or flywheels.

controls.title: Emergency Lighting
controls.statement: Employ and maintain automatic emergency lighting for the system that activates in the event of a power outage or disruption and that covers emergency exits and evacuation routes within the facility.
controls.discussion: Automatic emergency lighting systems illuminate for at least 90 minutes per NFPA requirements after main power failure. Emergency lighting systems may include emergency exit signs for evacuation routes.

controls.title: Fire Protection
controls.statement: Employ and maintain fire detection and suppression systems for the system.
controls.discussion: Fire detection and suppression systems that may be used to satisfy this control include sprinkler systems, gaseous suppression systems, and fire extinguishers. Organizations consider issues including the placement and operation of automatic suppression systems, the activation of systems without human intervention, and the potential damage to organizational assets from suppression agents (e.g., water damage resulting from sprinklers).

controls.title: Environmental Controls

items.label: PE-14a: Maintain [Selection (one or more): temperature; humidity; pressure; radiation; [Assignment: organization-defined environmental control]] levels within the facility where the system resides at [Assignment: organization-defined acceptable levels]; and
items.text: Maintain [Selection (one or more): temperature; humidity; pressure; radiation; [Assignment: organization-defined environmental control]] levels within the facility where the system resides at [Assignment: organization-defined acceptable levels]; and

items.label: PE-14b: Monitor environmental control levels [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].
items.text: Monitor environmental control levels [Assignment: organization-defined frequency].

controls.discussion: This control applies primarily to facilities containing concentrations of system resources including data centers, server rooms, and mainframe computer rooms. Temperature and humidity controls also apply to systems in operational environments.

controls.title: Water Damage Protection
controls.statement: Protect the system from damage resulting from water leakage by providing master shutoff or isolation valves that are accessible, working properly, and known to key personnel.
controls.discussion: This control applies to organizational facilities that contain concentrations of system resources including data centers, server rooms, and mainframe computer rooms. Protecting systems from water damage resulting from broken plumbing lines or other sources of water leakage can be accomplished by relocating systems, protecting systems with covers, installing drainage, or by monitoring for water leakage.

controls.title: Delivery and Removal

items.label: PE-16a: Authorize and control [Assignment: organization-defined types of system components] entering and exiting the facility; and
items.text: Authorize and control [Assignment: organization-defined types of system components] entering and exiting the facility; and

items.label: PE-16b: Maintain records of the system components.
items.text: Maintain records of the system components.

controls.discussion: Movement of hardware into or out of the facility where it is used in organizational systems is tracked and documented, with appropriate authorizations obtained for such movement. Appropriate controls are applied to equipment within the facility to protect the equipment and information.

controls.title: Alternate Work Site

items.label: PE-17a: Determine and document the [Assignment: organization-defined alternate work sites] allowed for use by employees
items.text: Determine and document the [Assignment: organization-defined alternate work sites] allowed for use by employees

items.label: PE-17b: Employ the following controls at alternate work sites: [Assignment: organization-defined controls]
items.text: Employ the following controls at alternate work sites: [Assignment: organization-defined controls]

items.label: PE-17c: Assess the effectiveness of controls at alternate work sites; and
items.text: Assess the effectiveness of controls at alternate work sites; and

items.label: PE-17d: Provide a means for employees to communicate with information security and privacy personnel in case of incidents.
items.text: Provide a means for employees to communicate with information security and privacy personnel in case of incidents.

controls.discussion: An alternate work site may be a separate physical location or a remote connection to an internal network. Alternate work sites may include government facilities or provide connections to home offices, hotels, offices of business partners, or other locations. Organizations may define different security requirements for different categories of alternate work sites depending on the work being performed at those sites.

controls.title: Location of System Components
controls.statement: Position system components within the facility to minimize potential damage from [Assignment: organization-defined physical and environmental hazards] and to minimize the opportunity for unauthorized access.
controls.discussion: The placement of system components in buildings or other structures considers both the environment and related factors (e.g., proximity to sources of heat, humidity, vibration, and electromagnetic fields as well as windows and exterior doors). Systems can be placed strategically to minimize risk from physical and environmental hazards while also minimizing opportunity for unauthorized physical access. Data centers in particular need careful placement to reduce access concerns.

controls.title: Information Leakage
controls.statement: Protect the system from information leakage due to electromagnetic signals emanations.
controls.discussion: An organizational assessment of risk guides the selection of controls to prevent information leakage. Protection from leakage due to electromagnetic signals emanations includes shielded enclosures (i.e., Faraday cages) and separation of equipment from electromagnetic shielding.

controls.title: Asset Monitoring and Tracking
controls.statement: Employ [Assignment: organization-defined asset location technologies] to track and monitor the location and movement of [Assignment: organization-defined assets] within [Assignment: organization-defined controlled areas].
controls.discussion: The assets tracked are organization-specific. Asset monitoring and tracking technologies can include Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) tags, Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, barcodes, and related readers or scanners. Organizations can use these technologies to track and monitor assets inside controlled areas and to detect unauthorized removal of assets from those areas.

controls.title: Electromagnetic Pulse Protection
controls.statement: Employ [Assignment: organization-defined electromagnetic pulse protection measures] for [Assignment: organization-defined systems and system components].
controls.discussion: An electromagnetic pulse (EMP) is a burst of electromagnetic energy. EMPs can be natural (lightning) or human-made (nuclear EMP or high altitude nuclear EMP). Organizations may consider the EMP threat when hardening critical systems, especially for continuity-of-operations (COOP) and disaster recovery (DR) scenarios.

controls.title: Component Marking
controls.statement: Mark [Assignment: organization-defined system hardware components] indicating the impact level or classification level of the information permitted to be processed, stored, or transmitted by the hardware component.
controls.discussion: Marking ensures that appropriate access controls are maintained throughout the system and that information is handled at the appropriate sensitivity level, especially where systems containing information at different sensitivity levels are physically co-located.

controls.title: Facility Location

items.label: PE-23a: Plan the location or site of the facility where the system resides considering physical and environmental hazards; and
items.text: Plan the location or site of the facility where the system resides considering physical and environmental hazards; and

items.label: PE-23b: For existing facilities, consider the physical and environmental hazards in the organizational risk management strategy.
items.text: For existing facilities, consider the physical and environmental hazards in the organizational risk management strategy.

controls.discussion: This control focuses on the layout and management of facilities from a security perspective. Addressing overall facility and infrastructure issues outside the scope of typical physical access controls, organizations consider the alignment of physical security with the information security program.

controls.title: System Security and Privacy Plans
controls.objective_name: PL-2: System Security and Privacy Plans

items.label: PL-2a: Develop security and privacy plans for the system that: 1. Are consistent with the organization’s enterprise architecture; 2. Explicitly define the constituent system components; 3. Describe the operational context of the system in terms of mission and business processes; 4. Identify the individuals that fulfill system roles and responsibilities; 5. Identify the information types processed, stored, and transmitted by the system; 6. Provide the security categorization of the system, including supporting rationale; 7. Describe any specific threats to the system that are of concern to the organization; 8. Provide the results of a privacy risk assessment for systems processing personally identifiable information; 9. Describe the operational environment for the system and any dependencies on or connections to other systems or system components; 10. Provide an overview of the security and privacy requirements for the system; 11. Identify any relevant control baselines or overlays, if applicable; 12. Describe the controls in place or planned for meeting the security and privacy requirements, including a rationale for any tailoring decisions; 13. Security plans also describe, at a high level, how the security controls and control enhancements meet those security requirements, but do not provide detailed, technical descriptions of the design or implementation of the controls/enhancements. Security plans contain sufficient information to enable a design and implementation that is unambiguously compliant with the intent of the plans and subsequently enable a security assessment of those controls/enhancements.

items.text: Establish and provide to individuals requiring access to the system, the rules that describe their responsibilities and expected behavior for information and system usage, security, and privacy

items.text: Receive a documented acknowledgment from such individuals, indicating that they have read, understand, and agree to abide by the rules of behavior, before authorizing access to information and the system

items.text: Develop a Concept of Operations (CONOPS) for the system describing how the organization intends to operate the system from the perspective of information security and privacy; and

Organizations define the types of evidence that might be generated in insider threat programs and use such programs to detect potential compromises of systems.

Describe how the architectures are integrated into and support the enterprise architecture; and 4. Describe any assumptions about, and dependencies on, external systems and services
items.text: Develop security and privacy architectures for the system that: 1.
